premise: A lone Minecraft player enters an impossible portal and is carried through different moments of his own single-player world. After witnessing the future destruction of his homestead, he tries to change events before discovering that his older self built the portal and that every intervention has always been part of one fixed timeline.
viewer_promise: A layered, fair time-travel mystery in which the journey begins after the portal is crossed. Familiar Minecraft spaces and actions become clues, allowing attentive viewers to infer that the unseen builder and interfering traveller are the protagonist himself before the final confirmation.
expected_pleasure: Uncanny recognition, causal deduction, reinterpreting earlier images, anticipating the self-builder revelation, and debating whether choice still matters when an observed outcome cannot change.
hook: A player finds a lit portal in a private cave where no portal existed, hesitates, then enters. He emerges into the same ravine in a state that cannot belong to the present, turning the portal’s origin into the first layer of a larger temporal mystery.
dramatic_engine: The connected questions ‘Who built the portal?’, ‘When is this version of the world?’ and ‘Can the foretold destruction be prevented?’ drive investigation and action. Each crossing reveals a new state of the same locations, while the protagonist’s attempts to interfere create the evidence he previously misunderstood.
thematic_question: If an outcome cannot be rewritten, can a choice still matter?
minecraft_causality: Single-player authorship makes the constructed portal impossible; persistent blocks preserve evidence across time; repeated ravine and homestead geography lets viewers recognise one world in several states; and verified survival mechanics must cause the destructive outcome and constrain the final rescue. The portal’s temporal behaviour is explicit invented canon rather than a claimed vanilla mechanic.
climactic_choice: Once he understands that the homestead’s destruction is fixed, the protagonist must choose whether to keep fighting for the structure or use the remaining time to rescue his tamed wolf. He abandons the futile objective and saves the relationship, an action that was always part of the observed history.
ending: The protagonist arrives before his original discovery and builds the portal he remembers entering, revealing himself as the unknown architect. He watches his younger self cross it, then later confronts the foretold destruction. The homestead still burns, but he rescues the wolf and understands that he participated in the fixed outcome rather than creating a replacement timeline.
final_state: The timeline and the burned landscape are unchanged. The portal mystery is solved, the protagonist has lost his home but not the wolf, and he leaves with a more mature understanding that agency can determine what an inevitable event means even when it cannot erase the event.
research_reason: The fixed-timeline premise benefits from limited conceptual research into the distinction between changing and participating in a single past and the proposed principle of self-consistency. Scholarly sources support a coherent fictional rule set but do not establish physical time travel. Minecraft-version research is deferred until the exact destructive mechanism is chosen.
